events.title: Phrack hacker zine first published
events.summary: The first issue of Phrack was published on November 17, 1985 — an electronic magazine that became the technical bible of the 1980s–1990s hacker underground.
events.about: Phrack published exploit techniques, Unix internals, and legal commentary — including the Hacker Manifesto and early CERT advisories. Its editors (Taran King, Knight Lightning, and later Erik Bloodaxe) shaped how security researchers shared knowledge before blogs and CVE databases existed.

narrative.whyChosen: Phrack was the definitive technical zine of the pre-web hacker era.
narrative.whyImportant: It documented vulnerabilities and culture in one archive researchers still cite.
narrative.problemSolved: Hackers on BBSes needed a centralized, persistent technical journal beyond ephemeral message boards.

events.title: Warez scene group Razor 1911 founded
events.summary: The software cracking group Razor 1911 formed in November 1985 — one of the oldest and most prolific teams in the warez and demoscene underground.
events.about: Razor 1911 shipped cracked games and applications with branded ASCII art intros and .NFO files — a template every scene release followed. Their competition with groups like Fairlight and CLASS drove faster cracks, tougher DRM battles, and the BBS/FTP topsite infrastructure that preceded BitTorrent piracy.

narrative.whyChosen: Razor 1911 is the most storied name in PC warez and game-cracking history.
narrative.whyImportant: Scene release standards (.NFO, crack intros, topsites) influenced how underground software distribution organized.
narrative.problemSolved: This was illicit distribution — it exposed how copy protection motivated an parallel reverse-engineering economy.
